articleHeadline: What Is Mpox (Monkeypox)?
articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox) is a viral disease with two clades: Congo Basin (up to 10% mortality) and West African (about 1% mortality; the 2022 outbreak). There is no mpox-specific approved treatment; antivirals developed for smallpox may help, usually reserved for immunocompromised patients: cidofovir, brincidovir (Tembexa), and tecovirimat (Tpoxx). Incubation is 5–21 days; initial flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, muscle aches, lymphadenopathy, fatigue) precede a rash that begins on the face and spreads to the hands and feet. Transmission occurs through close contact with infected people or animals, including respiratory secretions, lesions, or contaminated materials; animal exposure includes bites, scratches, meat, or products. Pregnant individuals can pass the virus to a fetus. Diagnosis relies on PCR from lesion samples. Vaccines: JYNNEOS (two-dose, approved 2019; up to 85% effective; effective within four days of exposure) and ACAM2000 (single-dose). Mpox is typically self-limiting in 14–21 days, though severe disease and complications can occur, especially in children.

articleSummary: 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were caused by infections, about 12% of all new cancers, according to IARC using 2024 GLOBOCAN data. The largest shares were linked to Helicobacter pylori (approximately 760,000 cases, mostly gastric cancer) and human papillomavirus (HPV) around 750,000 cases, driving nearly all cervical cancer and portions of anal, genital, and oropharyngeal cancers. About 360,000 cases were associated with hepatitis B virus (HBV), 260,000 with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and 160,000 with hepatitis C virus (HCV). These five infections account for the majority of infection-attributable cancers. EBV is newly linked to gastric cancer in this update. Infection itself is not contagious; infections raise cancer risk via chronic inflammation, cellular damage, or immune changes. East Asia bears the largest burden (~990,000 cases, 42%). Prevention includes HPV and HBV vaccination, HCV antiviral therapy, H. pylori testing and treatment, HIV management, safe injections, condom use, and HPV-related precancer screening.

Moto-taxi drivers and market sellers were targeted to increase uptake of mask use and gel. articleHeadline: 1 in 8 Cancer Cases Worldwide Are Linked to Infections
articleSummary: In 2024, about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide were linked to infections, roughly 12% of all cancers. The five infections accounted for most cases: Helicobacter pylori ≈760,000 (4%), human papillomavirus ≈750,000 (4%), hepatitis B ≈360,000, Epstein-Barr virus ≈260,000, and hepatitis C ≈160,000. East Asia bore the largest burden with ≈990,000 infection-related cancers (42% of the global total), and more than three-quarters of cases occurred in low- and middle-income countries. Prevention opportunities include HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, HIV testing and treatment, H. pylori testing and treatment, and hepatitis B and C management, along with safer injection practices, condoms/HIV PrEP, and screening for precancerous cervical and anal changes linked to HPV. EBV has no vaccine or approved antiviral; HIV can drive AIDS-related cancers. Stronger infection control could avert many cancers.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is caused by Bundibugyo virus, with 8,300 confirmed cases and 4,018 deaths (case fatality ~48.4%), surpassing the 2018–2020 outbreak. Declared May 15, 2026 in Ituri province after Bundibugyo virus disease cases were identified, initially in Mongbwalu. By Sept 25, transmission had spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces: Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud-Ubangi and Tshopo. WHO notes the surge amid insecurity, displacement, and limited health access. Bundibugyo, a less-studied Orthoebolavirus, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment; current response is supportive care. As of Sept 23, WHO reported 7,890 cases and 3,799 deaths. Vaccines like Ervebo (Zaire ebolavirus) are being explored in trials for potential cross-protection, but efficacy against Bundibugyo is unproven. Transmission requires contact with infected bodily fluids; early symptoms mimic malaria, typhoid, and meningitis; lab confirmation is essential.

articleHeadline: Fever Turns the Tables on Sleeping Sickness Parasites, Study Finds
articleSummary: Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind African sleeping sickness, is sensitive to fever; in C57BL/6J mice, parasitaemia rises around day 3 post-infection, with fever (days 4–5) coinciding with the rise of the short, transmission-ready stumpy form. Stumpy cells peak at ~75% of parasites, then collapse by day 7 as temperatures normalize. In vitro, stumpy cells survive at tsetse-mimicking 27°C but die rapidly at 39°C; slender forms tolerate heat better. Fever dramatically enhances clearance when combined with antibodies: day-21 plasma plus heat eradicates >99.5% of stumpy cells within 24 h, versus 15–18% survival with either alone. Heat triggers apoptosis-like events via mitochondrial pathways, including upregulation of Metacasp-3, mitochondrial damage, and oxidative stress; >43% show mitochondrial perturbation after 24 h at 37°C, rising to >95% at 39°C. The work, from Sun Yat-sen University and University of Salford, refines view of host fever as a driver of remission during early infection.

articleHeadline: Clean Chemistry, Hidden Germs: Ghana's Boreholes Reveal a Groundwater
articleSummary: Sixteen boreholes supplying domestic water in Segyemase, Juaso, and Nsuapemso in Ghana's Eastern Region appear chemically pristine (pH 5.38–7.29, conduct. ~173.5 μS/cm, TDS ~135 mg/L; fluoride below 1.5 mg/L). Yet microbiological testing found faecal coliforms and Escherichia coli in two boreholes, implying potential infection risk with an annual probability up to about 58% for the worst source. The study, published in Discover Geoscience, used an integrated framework combining hydrochemical characterization, six water quality/pollution indices, microbiological indicators, ecological risk diagnostics, and quantitative microbial risk assessment; samples were collected September 2022 during the late wet season and analyzed at CSIR-WRI Accra per APHA methods. Hydrochemistry indicates groundwater from Proterozoic Birimian rocks dominated by carbonate dissolution and silicate weathering, with pH strongly linked to bicarbonate (r=0.97) and iron to manganese (r=0.90). Composite indices correlated highly; trace metals pollution index showed a more complex story.

The N-PDF is a competitive national fellowship supporting high-quality work in animal and public health within the One Health domain. T. gondii infection in sheep and goats can cause abortion, fetal death, stillbirth, and weak offspring; cats are definitive hosts, with oocysts contaminating soil, water, feed, and food. Humans may acquire infection via contaminated food/water, poorly washed vegetables, or undercooked meat, and congenital toxoplasmosis can affect eyes, brain, and nervous system. The project aims to identify proteins and molecular markers and study environmental survival and infectivity to aid surveillance, diagnosis, and control.

articleHeadline: Rare Fungal Brain Infection Reveals Striking Christmas-Tree Sign on MRI
articleSummary: As of 3 October 2026 in Hangzhou, China, a 50-year-old woman with hydrocephalus developed intracranial talaromycosis due to Talaromyces marneffei. The infection progressed from meningitis to widespread vasculitis and multiple hemorrhagic cerebral infarcts. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed skull-base meningitis with a Christmas-tree-like pattern and irregular vessel-wall enhancement and luminal irregularities, implicating vasculitis in which vascular occlusion led to infarcts and hemorrhagic transformation. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid and blood confirmed T. marneffei, a thermally dimorphic fungus endemic to Southeast Asia and southern China. CNS involvement is rare, historically seen in HIV-infected individuals but increasingly reported in HIV-negative patients. After induction therapy with liposomal amphotericin B 150 mg daily for two weeks, consciousness did not improve, suggesting irreversible vascular/parenchymal damage and antifungal-refractory fungal vasculitis. Prior empiric piperacillin-tazobactam did not target the fungus.

articleSummary: Rabies remains incurable once clinical symptoms appear, making post-bite management critical. Experts emphasize administering rabies vaccine and rabies immune serum after suspected exposure to a rabid animal. The vaccine enables antibody development, typically taking one to two weeks; the serum helps neutralize the virus when it is suspected to have entered the body. In some cases, vaccines and serum may be given together based on medical judgment. Rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms start, reflecting CNS involvement including the brain. The incubation period averages two to three months but can range from weeks to over a year. Do not wait for symptoms; first aid includes washing the wound with running water and soap, then seeking medical care.
